_doc: High school story graph (HS_001-HS_160), generated by tools/convert_hs_graph.py from tools/hs_graph/high_school_scenarios.json. Same fields as scenarios_hs.json (see its _doc). 'draft': true = no content yet, never picked. 'expected_flags' = flags some choice must set (checked once the draft flag is removed). 'authoring' = notes for writers (unlocked_by, leads_to, choice_locks, follow_up_hints); the game ignores it. Edit category/text/choices here; change graph fields via the converter's decision tables.

scenarios.title: The New Kid
scenarios.text: It's your first week at the high school, and the lunchroom feels like it already has its own seating chart. A few players from the football team wave you over, but you don't know them yet.

choices.label: Join the football table
choices.result: You sit with the team and learn everyone's names. The conversation is awkward at first, but a couple of players make room for you.

choices.label: Introduce yourself to someone new
choices.result: You strike up a conversation with another student who is also finding their way around. It feels good to make a connection outside football.

choices.label: Find a quiet spot and review the playbook
choices.result: You spend lunch learning the team's terminology. You feel more prepared at practice, even if you haven't made many friends yet.

scenarios.title: Homework or the Field?
scenarios.text: Your math assignment is due tomorrow, but the field is open and the kickers are getting extra reps. You know you can't put off the homework forever.

choices.label: Finish the assignment first
choices.result: You miss some extra kicks, but turn in work you're proud of. Your teacher notices you took the deadline seriously.

choices.label: Get extra kicks in before studying
choices.result: You get valuable reps while the field is quiet, then work through the assignment later than planned.

scenarios.title: The Locker Room Joke
scenarios.text: A few upperclassmen hide a freshman's practice gear and laugh as he searches the locker room. One of them nudges you to join in.

choices.label: Step in and help him find it
choices.result: The laughing dies down. One senior rolls his eyes, but the freshman gives you a grateful nod on the way out.

choices.label: Laugh along with the upperclassmen
choices.result: The older players welcome you into the joke, but the freshman stops looking your way. You can tell he won't forget it.

choices.label: Don't join in; quietly return his gear
choices.result: You avoid turning it into a bigger scene and make sure he gets his things back. The seniors move on, though you haven't challenged them directly.

scenarios.title: Dad's Expectations
scenarios.text: After practice, {parent} says he knows you can become the best kicker on the team. He means it as encouragement, but lately every conversation seems to turn into what you need to improve.

choices.label: Tell {parent} how the pressure feels
choices.result: You explain that you appreciate the support but need room to make mistakes. {parent} listens, even if the conversation is a little uncomfortable.

choices.label: Ask {parent} to help set realistic goals
choices.result: You sit down together and make a simple plan for practice. The expectations feel more manageable when you have a say in them.

choices.label: Change the subject for now
choices.result: {parent} keeps talking about your next game. You avoid an argument tonight, but the pressure doesn't really go away.

scenarios.title: The First Rival
scenarios.text: {tyler}, the other freshman kicker, drills four straight from forty yards on the first day of practice. He catches you watching and says, "Hope you're ready to compete."

choices.label: Ask him to train together
choices.result: {tyler} seems surprised, then agrees. You split the net and trade pointers until practice ends. The competition suddenly feels more useful than personal.

choices.label: Tell him you'll take the starting job
choices.result: {tyler} grins and fires back that he'll see you at tryouts. The challenge lights a fire under you, though the two of you aren't exactly friends.

scenarios.title: The Party Invitation
scenarios.text: An older teammate invites you to a party Saturday night. Half the team is going, it's across town, and the only ride home leaves whenever the upperclassmen do.

choices.label: Go and stay till the end
choices.result: You laugh with the team until the ride finally heads out after midnight. You drag through the rest of the weekend, but on Monday people talk to you like you've always been around.

choices.label: Go, but line up your own ride
choices.result: You hang out for a couple of hours, then text {parent} for a pickup at ten. A few upperclassmen tease you for leaving early, but you still get a full night's sleep.

choices.label: Pass on it this time
choices.result: You say thanks but you're worn out from the week. You wake up rested, then spend Monday hearing inside jokes you weren't there for.

scenarios.title: The Group Project
scenarios.text: You're paired with two classmates on a science project due the same week as a road game. One partner hasn't answered a single message, and the other suggests splitting it three ways and hoping for the best.

choices.label: Take charge of the project
choices.result: You set a schedule, hand out the parts and stay up late finishing the slides. The project earns a solid grade, though you're running on fumes by game day.

choices.label: Split it and do your part
choices.result: You finish your third and leave the rest to them. The silent partner turns in something rushed at the last minute, and the grade comes back lower than you hoped.

choices.label: Tell your teacher what's happening
choices.result: You quietly let your science teacher know one partner has gone silent. The workload gets adjusted, but the partner figures out who said something and class gets awkward.

scenarios.title: The Missed Kick
scenarios.text: You miss a kick in practice that you normally make. The ball sails wide, and you can feel the other kickers watching to see how you'll respond.

choices.label: Stay after and review the miss
choices.result: You slow the rep down, check your plant foot, and work through a few controlled kicks. The extra effort helps you understand what went wrong.

choices.label: Shake it off and reset for tomorrow
choices.result: You pack up with the group instead of chasing one bad rep. A little distance helps you keep the miss from taking over your night.

choices.label: Get frustrated and rush a few more kicks
choices.result: You try to force the next few attempts, but your timing gets worse. By the time you stop, you're more annoyed than when you started.

scenarios.title: The Little Brother
scenarios.text: Your little brother {sibling} has been waiting all afternoon to show you a model football field he made. You have practice notes to review before tomorrow, and he keeps asking you to come look.

choices.label: Help him finish the field
choices.result: You set your notes aside and help line up the tiny goalposts. He beams when you take his project seriously, though your own evening gets tighter.

choices.label: Give him a little time
choices.result: You spend a few minutes checking out the field, then explain what you still need to do. He is a little disappointed, but you promise to look again tomorrow.

choices.label: Ask him to wait tonight
choices.result: You tell him you need to prepare for practice and head back to your notes. You get your work done, but he quietly puts the field away.

scenarios.title: The First School Dance
scenarios.text: The first school dance is Friday, and {love_interest} asks if you are going. You want to spend time together, but the crowded gym and the thought of asking someone to dance make you nervous.

choices.label: Ask them to go together
choices.result: You ask if they want to arrive together, and they smile before saying yes. You still feel nervous, but having a plan makes the dance feel exciting.

choices.label: Meet up at the dance
choices.result: You say you'll see them there and keep the invitation casual. It takes some pressure off, though you both spend part of the night trying to find each other.

choices.label: Skip the dance this time
choices.result: You explain that big crowds aren't really your thing and suggest talking at school instead. They understand, even if you both wish the timing had worked out.

scenarios.title: The Teacher Who Believes in You
scenarios.text: {teacher} notices your grades slipping once the season gets busy and asks you to stay after class. You have real potential, you're told, and there's still time to build a plan before things get harder.

choices.label: Make a study plan together
choices.result: You work out a schedule for assignments around practice. It takes some free time, but you leave knowing exactly what needs to get done.

choices.label: Ask for help on one subject
choices.result: You admit which class is giving you trouble and go over the next assignment. The smaller commitment feels manageable, and you leave with a better starting point.

choices.label: Say you can handle it
choices.result: You say thanks and promise to catch up on your own. You keep your afternoon free, but the missing work is still waiting when you get home.

scenarios.title: The New Teammate
scenarios.text: A new player joins the team and looks lost while everyone else gets ready for practice. He ends up beside you during warmups, unsure where to go or what the coaches expect.

choices.label: Show him the routine
choices.result: You walk him through the warmup and explain where the kickers line up. It costs you a few minutes, but he settles in and practice starts smoothly.

choices.label: Invite him to warm up
choices.result: You make room beside you and let him follow your lead. You get your own routine done while giving him a chance to feel included.

choices.label: Focus on your own work
choices.result: You give him a quick nod and stick to your usual warmup. You stay on schedule, but he has to figure out the routine by watching everyone else.

scenarios.title: The Bad Weather Practice
scenarios.text: Cold rain rolls in an hour into practice. The coaches move the offense indoors, but say the kickers can stay out on the wet field if they want.

choices.label: Stay out and kick in the rain
choices.result: You kick until your cleats are caked in mud, learning how a wet ball comes off your foot. You go home soaked and shivering, but bad-weather kicks feel a little less scary.

choices.label: Head inside and study film
choices.result: You join the offense indoors and watch your approach on the big screen. You spot a hitch in your plant step, but you don't get a single real rep in.

choices.label: Call it a day early
choices.result: You dry off, head home early and finish your homework before dinner. You feel rested, though you notice the other kickers stayed out the whole time.

scenarios.title: The Locker Room Rumor
scenarios.text: A rumor goes around the locker room that a starting lineman is about to quit the team. A couple of guys ask you if it's true, since you sat next to him on the bus.

choices.label: Ask him directly
choices.result: You find him after practice and ask how he's doing. The rumor is mostly wrong: he's dealing with something at home, and he's glad someone asked instead of guessing.

choices.label: Tell them to drop it
choices.result: You say you don't know anything and they should leave it alone. The talk cools off around you, even if it keeps going elsewhere.

choices.label: Share what you noticed
choices.result: You mention he seemed quiet on the bus, and by lunch the story has doubled. You're in on the conversation for a day, but when he hears where it started, he stops saving you a seat.

scenarios.title: The Scholarship Camp Flyer
scenarios.text: A flyer on the locker room board advertises a weekend kicking camp where college coaches sometimes stop by. It costs more than you'd like to ask your family for, and it lands on a friend's birthday weekend.

choices.label: Ask your family to help pay
choices.result: Your family agrees, though you can tell it's a stretch, and you miss the birthday to go. You get two days of coached reps and a nod from one of the camp staff.

choices.label: Save up for next year's camp
choices.result: You decide to earn the money yourself and go next summer. You make the birthday, and the plan feels like your own.

choices.label: Study free videos instead
choices.result: You spend a few evenings breaking down free kicking videos online. It costs nothing, but there's nobody there to correct your form.

scenarios.title: The Coach's Favorite
scenarios.text: {coach} asks you to stay after practice for extra attention on your approach and follow-through. A couple of teammates notice and joke that you must be the coach's favorite.

choices.label: Take the extra coaching
choices.result: You stay and work through the details with {coach}, getting several focused reps in. You improve your routine, but the extra attention leaves your legs tired.

choices.label: Invite a teammate to join
choices.result: You ask if another kicker can stay too, turning the extra time into a shared session. You get useful reps and keep the atmosphere from feeling exclusive.

choices.label: Thank coach and head out
choices.result: You tell {coach} you appreciate the offer but need to recover tonight. You miss the extra instruction, but arrive home with more energy for tomorrow.

scenarios.title: The Broken Phone
scenarios.text: Your phone slips out of your bag at practice and the screen shatters. A repair costs money you don't have, and the team chat and every assignment reminder run through that phone.

choices.label: Earn the repair money
choices.result: You trade a few weeks of yard work and extra chores for the repair. You're worn out, but the fixed phone feels earned.

choices.label: Live with the cracks
choices.result: You squint through the broken screen for a few weeks and keep your weekends free. It mostly works, but you miss a couple of messages about practice changes.

choices.label: Take a break from your phone
choices.result: You leave it in a drawer and go without for a couple of weeks. You sleep better and focus in class, though you're out of the loop on weekend plans.

authoring.ungated: Open to everyone; the unlock flags are flavor only.

scenarios.title: The Rival's Bad Day
scenarios.text: You and {tyler} have trained together since freshman year, so you know how much the competition matters to both of you. After a rough practice, {tyler} misses several kicks and starts packing up in frustration.

choices.label: Offer to work through it
choices.result: You stay and help {tyler} break down the approach and reset the routine. It takes extra time, but the session turns into the kind of honest competition that makes both of you better.

choices.label: Give him room today
choices.result: You tell {tyler} everyone has rough practices and let him head out on his own. You keep your own evening free, but the two of you miss a chance to turn the bad day around together.

scenarios.title: The Friend Who Needs Help
scenarios.text: The freshman you stood up for last year catches you after practice: your best friend {best_friend} has been struggling with something at school and won't say what. You can tell it's weighing on {best_friend}, but you don't know the whole story.

choices.label: Listen before giving advice
choices.result: You make time to hear what has been going on and help {best_friend} sort out the next step. The conversation takes energy, but they leave feeling less alone.

choices.label: Help solve one problem
choices.result: You help {best_friend} tackle the most urgent part instead of trying to fix everything at once. It feels practical and gives you both a little breathing room, though some of the bigger worries remain.

choices.label: Keep your distance for now
choices.result: You say you have a lot going on and suggest talking to a trusted adult at school. You protect your own time, but {best_friend} seems disappointed that you aren't more available.

scenarios.title: The Rival's Offer
scenarios.text: After the respect you built by helping {tyler} through a rough practice, he approaches you after school with an idea: train together for an upcoming skills showcase. You know working side by side could help both of you, but it may also sharpen the competition.

choices.label: Train together
choices.result: You agree to share a structured session, taking turns calling out small adjustments and pushing each other through the final reps. The work is demanding, but you both leave sharper.

choices.label: Set friendly boundaries
choices.result: You tell {tyler} you're glad to work together occasionally, but want most of your training time to stay independent. He understands, though the distance takes some of the excitement out of the idea.

choices.label: Turn it into a challenge
choices.result: You accept, but make it clear you want to see who can outwork the other. The competitive edge makes the session intense; afterward, the two of you are less relaxed around each other.

scenarios.title: The Breakup Before the Big Game
The Final Exam Versus the Final Game

scenarios.title: The Teammate Who Wants Your Spot
The Final Rivalry
scenarios.text: With the final stretch of senior season approaching, {tyler} is still the rival who knows exactly how to get under your skin. A few teammates bring up the competition between you, and you have to decide what you want these last weeks to mean.

choices.label: Let the rivalry fuel you
choices.result: You channel the tension into a focused routine and keep your attention on the work in front of you. The edge gives you energy, but it is harder to switch off afterward.

choices.label: Make peace before it ends
choices.result: You speak with {tyler} privately and say you don't want the season to end with bitterness. The conversation doesn't erase the past, but it eases the tension and gives you some perspective.

choices.label: Avoid the conversation
choices.result: You keep your distance and let the others talk. It saves you from another uncomfortable exchange, but the unresolved tension follows you through the week.

scenarios.title: The Teammate Who Remembers
scenarios.text: A classmate you stood up for as a freshman recognizes you in the hallway. He says he still remembers that you helped when older students hid his gear, and asks how you've been handling the pressure this year.

choices.label: Catch up with him
choices.result: You make time to listen and share a little about your own year. The conversation lifts both your spirits, even though you arrive at your next stop feeling behind.

choices.label: Offer practical advice
choices.result: You talk through ways to handle team pressure and school responsibilities. He leaves with a plan, and you feel good about helping, though the advice takes more out of you than expected.

choices.label: Keep it brief
choices.result: You give him a friendly greeting and say you have to get moving. You protect your time, but the quick exchange feels a little distant after he made the effort to find you.

scenarios.title: The Wrong Locker
scenarios.text: You open your locker and find someone else's books inside. An older student steps over, says you took his locker, and starts raising his voice as other students watch.

choices.label: Stay calm and sort it out
choices.result: You explain which locker number is on your schedule and offer to check with the office together. The mix-up gets cleared up without a scene, and the older student backs off.

choices.label: Snap back at him
choices.result: You tell him to prove it and raise your voice too. He eventually walks away, but the hallway turns into an audience and the disagreement follows you into class.

scenarios.title: The Open Gym
scenarios.text: The school opens the gym after classes, and a few players are setting up a kicking station. You have time to join them, but you also have homework and a chance to take the afternoon easy.

choices.label: Join the kicking session
choices.result: You take turns kicking into the practice net and get pointers on your approach. The extra reps sharpen your routine, though you get home later than planned.

choices.label: Save the afternoon
choices.result: You head home instead and get your assignments finished before relaxing. Your legs feel fresh the next day, but you miss a chance to get extra work in.

scenarios.title: The First Group Chat
scenarios.text: A group chat starts making fun of a teammate after an awkward moment at practice, and the jokes keep piling up. You know the teammate will probably see the messages, and everyone in the chat can see what you do next.

choices.label: Tell them to knock it off
choices.result: You say the jokes have gone too far and ask the group to leave the teammate alone. A few people go quiet, but you feel better knowing you didn't let it slide.

choices.label: Check in privately
choices.result: You message the teammate directly and let them know you saw the chat and don't agree with it. They appreciate hearing from you, even though the group chat carries on without you stepping in publicly.

choices.label: Join in with the jokes
choices.result: You add a joke of your own, and the chat fills with laughing reactions. It feels easy to fit in for the moment, but the teammate stops talking when you see them at practice.

scenarios.title: The Family Road Trip
scenarios.text: Your family has planned a road trip for the same weekend as your first kicking clinic. {parent} says the trip matters to everyone, while the clinic could give you a chance to learn from experienced kickers.

choices.label: Take the family trip
choices.result: You go on the trip and enjoy having everyone together without thinking about practice for a couple of days. You miss the clinic, but {parent} appreciates that you made the family plans a priority.

choices.label: Attend the kicking clinic
choices.result: You explain why the clinic matters and travel there while your family heads out. You get valuable instruction and several focused reps, though you miss the shared trip and {parent} is disappointed.

choices.label: Work out a split weekend
choices.result: You attend part of the clinic, then meet your family for the rest of the trip. You don't get the full clinic experience, but you still learn a few things and make time for everyone.

scenarios.title: The Substitute Holder
scenarios.text: Your usual holder, {holder}, is unavailable for part of practice, and a backup is filling in. The backup is still learning how to place the ball and time the snap, so you can either help them get comfortable or stick to your own routine.

choices.label: Help train the backup holder
choices.result: You slow things down and work through the snap, spot, and timing together. It takes time away from your own kicks, but the backup starts getting the ball down more consistently.

choices.label: Stick with your own routine
choices.result: You ask to keep your reps moving and let the coaches handle the backup's instruction. You get more kicks in, but the backup is still unsure about the timing when practice ends.

scenarios.title: The First Volunteer Day
scenarios.text: A community volunteer day is coming up, and organizers need help setting up a youth sports field before the weekend games. You can commit to the full morning or stop by for a shorter shift around your other plans.

choices.label: Commit to the full morning
choices.result: You spend the morning moving equipment, setting up cones, and getting the field ready. You're worn out by the end, but the organizers are grateful you stayed until the work was done.

choices.label: Help for a shorter shift
choices.result: You arrive early, help unload supplies, and stay until the main setup is finished. You have time for the rest of your day, though you leave before the final cleanup.

scenarios.title: The First Time You're Recognized
scenarios.text: After a kick that gets the sideline cheering, a school photographer asks for a quick picture and a few words about it. Teammates nearby are still celebrating, and you have to decide how to handle the attention.

choices.label: Give the team the credit
choices.result: You mention the snap, the hold, and the teammates who helped you prepare. The photographer gets a good quote, and your teammates appreciate that you included them in the moment.

choices.label: Enjoy the attention
choices.result: You smile for the camera and talk about how much the kick means to you. The attention feels great, though a couple of teammates think you could have mentioned the work everyone put in.

choices.label: Keep it low-key
choices.result: You tell the photographer it was just one kick and that there's plenty of work left to do. You avoid the spotlight, but some classmates read your answer as brushing off a moment they were excited to celebrate.

scenarios.title: The Starting Job Is in Question
The Hallway Favor
scenarios.text: After you calmly settled that locker mix-up as a freshman, a younger student approaches you in the hallway with a similar problem: an older student keeps telling them they don't belong in a certain part of the team area. They ask what you would do.

choices.label: Walk them through it
choices.result: You help the student explain the situation clearly and offer to go with them to the office or coach. It costs part of your break, but they leave with a plan and more confidence.

choices.label: Point them to an adult
choices.result: You encourage them to speak with a coach or school staff member who can sort out the issue properly. You keep your own schedule on track, though the student has to take the next step without you beside them.

scenarios.title: The Community Recognition
scenarios.text: The organizers of the youth sports field project remember that you stayed for the full setup morning a couple of years ago. They invite you back to help at a community event, and a few people mention how much that earlier effort meant.

choices.label: Accept the recognition
choices.result: You thank the organizers and share how good it feels to see the field full of young players. You spend more time talking with families than you planned, but the community connection grows.

choices.label: Get back to helping
choices.result: You thank them briefly and return to setting up equipment, keeping the focus on the kids and the event. You avoid the attention and get useful work done, though you miss a chance to build those community connections.

scenarios.title: The Screenshot
scenarios.text: The group chat you once challenged for mocking a teammate comes up again when someone shares an old screenshot. A few people start arguing about what happened, and you realize your earlier message is part of the conversation.

choices.label: Own what you said
choices.result: You explain why you spoke up and make it clear you still think the jokes crossed a line. The discussion gets uncomfortable, but your teammates know you haven't changed your position.

choices.label: Let the chat move on
choices.result: You don't respond and mute the conversation for the evening. You avoid another round of arguments, but people are left to guess whether you still stand by what you said.

authoring.note: A new offensive coordinator or position coach joins the staff; the head coach ({coach}) stays the same person. The newcomer has no relationship value or placeholder: name them in the text and keep the name consistent. rel 'coach' still means the head coach.

scenarios.title: The Holder's Big Moment
scenarios.text: The week of a big game, {holder} bobbles a few snaps at practice and teammates start joking about it. {holder} quietly asks whether you'd rather work with someone else.

choices.label: Settle in and trust them
choices.result: You give {holder} a calm nod and stay after practice to rep the hold until the ball goes down clean every time. By Thursday you're both locked in, and you make sure {holder} knows you'd want nobody else on the hold.

choices.label: Show your frustration
choices.result: You point out the bobbles in front of everyone. A few teammates agree with you, but {holder} goes quiet afterward, unsure whether you still trust them.

scenarios.title: The Starting Job Is Yours
scenarios.text: You've earned the starting job, and {tyler} knows it. After practice, the two of you have a quiet moment near the equipment room; whatever your history has been, this change puts your relationship at a crossroads.

choices.label: Recognize what he pushed you to do
choices.result: You tell {tyler} that the competition helped you grow and that you respect the work he put in. The conversation is awkward at first, but it ends with a more honest understanding between you.

choices.label: Keep competing together
choices.result: You suggest continuing to train together, with clear goals and no promises about who comes out ahead. {tyler} considers it, and the familiar challenge gives both of you something to work toward.

scenarios.title: The Unexpected Reference
scenarios.text: Someone in the community who has seen the effort you put in over time approaches you with an unexpected offer. They may be able to speak about your character and reliability, but they ask what kind of help you actually need.

choices.label: Accept their recommendation
choices.result: You thank them and accept the offer to serve as a reference. They point to the consistency they've seen from you, giving you a meaningful boost as you think about what comes next.

choices.label: Ask for specific guidance
choices.result: You explain what opportunity you're pursuing and ask what would make your application stronger. They agree to help you prepare, though you leave with a few more things to work on.

scenarios.title: The Younger Athlete Looks Up to You
scenarios.text: A younger athlete catches you after school and says they've noticed the way you carry yourself around the team and in the community. They ask how you stay steady when people are watching and others are counting on you.

choices.label: Take them under your wing
choices.result: You listen to their concerns and offer to check in with them from time to time. It takes some of your free time, but they leave encouraged and you realize your example matters.

choices.label: Give them a quick answer
choices.result: You share one practical piece of advice and encourage them to keep showing up for their work. You protect your afternoon, though the conversation ends before a real connection forms.

scenarios.title: A Family Thank-You
scenarios.text: As senior year gets busier, {parent} tells you how much your support has meant to the family over the years. The conversation turns to everything you've balanced together, and you realize there are things you haven't really said out loud.

choices.label: Talk openly with him
choices.result: You tell {parent} what the family's support has meant to you, and listen as he shares what he's been carrying too. The conversation takes time and brings up some difficult feelings, but you understand each other better.

choices.label: Keep things light tonight
choices.result: You thank {parent} and steer the conversation toward lighter topics. The evening stays comfortable and you get a chance to relax, though some important feelings remain unspoken.

scenarios.title: The Last Practice Together
scenarios.text: It's the last practice of your senior year. {coach} gathers the group while {holder} helps put away the equipment, and the familiar routine suddenly feels like something you'll miss; you have a chance to recognize the people who helped make it matter.

choices.label: Thank them for the support
choices.result: You thank {coach} for the guidance and {holder} for being someone you could count on. The words are simple, but both take them seriously, and the moment leaves the group feeling appreciated.

choices.label: Keep the moment to yourself
choices.result: You help finish putting everything away and let the others have their conversations. You avoid making a big emotional moment of it, though you leave with a little regret that you didn't say more.

authoring.beat_note: Always plays. Give one choice per lock flag (requires {flags: [flag]} + lock_text) and one open choice.
